8clerk8 video: Claude Fable 5.2 used computer use to paint a Victorian Christmas street in Microsoft Paint over about 2.5 hours (2 likes).

Anthropic’s new Fable 5.2 model draws in Microsoft Paint.

A model that builds operating systems and formalizes mathematical proofs was given a mouse and MS Paint.

No reference image. Just a text prompt: a detailed Victorian era Christmas street, looking down the road. It opened Paint through computer use in the Claude desktop app, then spent the next 2.5 hours painting it itself.

It didn’t dump pixels. It wrote mouse-movement scripts, took a screenshot after each pass, looked at what it had actually drawn, and planned the next layer. Broad strokes first, then smaller marks, then the details that make a street feel lived in. It mixed colors by clicking the picker. It corrected mistakes by painting over them. There was no undo.

The whole thing cost about $45 in API calls.

In the video the cursor moves like a careful, slightly hesitant hand. Lines appear. Windows get filled. Lights start to glow. The street slowly becomes a place. It keeps going long after a human would have gotten bored or impatient.

This is the same model that, days earlier, coordinated over a thousand subagents for eight days to write an operating system from an empty folder.

The same model that scores higher than GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Carbon on most of Anthropic’s hardest technical benchmarks.

It spent an afternoon on a Christmas street in Paint.

The model that can keep an agent session running for hours or days chose to sit with a brush tool and a color picker until the picture was finished. Is that the future of computer use, or just the most expensive MS Paint session in history?

Jack Prandelli video: why crude oil and diesel are two different markets, explained through fractional distillation (137 likes).

Jack Prandelli@jackprandelli
🛢️Why crude oil and diesel are 2 different markets?

Every barrel of crude goes through the same first step: fractional distillation.

The crude is heated and fed into a tall column.

The lighter parts rise and condense near the top and the heavier parts stay at the bottom.

Each level of the column gives a different product.

From top to bottom:

🔹 LPG
🔹 Petrol
🔹 Naphtha, for plastics and chemicals
🔹 Kerosene and jet fuel
🔹 Diesel
🔹 Heavy fuel oil
🔹 Bitumen and residue

The column only splits the crude into pieces.

Other units then crack and upgrade the heavier pieces into more of the valuable ones.

That second stage is what makes a refinery valuable.

The result: a 42-gallon barrel in a US refinery gives about 19–20 gallons of petrol, 11–13 gallons of diesel and 4 gallons of jet fuel.

The output is about 45 gallons in total, because the products are lighter than the crude they come from.

This matters a lot right now.

Crude can be rerouted around a war.
A refinery can’t be moved.

🇷🇺 Russia has lost so much refining to drone strikes that it now exports more crude and about 1/3 less fuel than a year ago.

The IEA says the market has a crude surplus while diesel is still the main concern.

Same barrel, same column, but the market for each product has gone its own way.

That’s the gap I follow in my latest article.
